historical_timeline.summary: Begins three seasons as Mr. Spock in Star Trek; later acts and directs in film.
Quits smoking, by his own account about thirty years before his 2014 announcement.
Announces publicly that he has COPD and urges smokers to quit.
Says he cannot walk distances; seen at an airport in a wheelchair.
Writes that an attempt to smoke a little failed and that he quit through a program; in March, that addiction made him ignore medical advice.
Died at home in Los Angeles; cause reported as end-stage COPD.

claims.statement: Leonard Nimoy was born in Boston on March 26, 1931.
He played Mr. Spock in the Star Trek television series from 1966 to 1969, later acted in and directed Star Trek films, and directed other films, including the comedy Three Men and a Baby.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Used for the synthetic modern occupation.

claims.statement: In a Twitter post at the end of January 2014 he announced that he had chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: "I quit smoking 30 yrs ago. Not soon enough. I have COPD. Grandpa says, quit now!! LLAP".
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own public disclosure of COPD and of having quit smoking about 30 years earlier. ABC News dates the post January 29 and TODAY dates it January 30; the case uses late January.

claims.statement: In early February 2014 he posted "I'm doing OK. Just can't walk distances," and ABC News reported that he had been seen at an airport in a wheelchair.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own public description of exertional limitation; used for the presenting concern.

claims.statement: In February 2014 he urged smokers to quit: "Smokers, please understand. If you quit after you're diagnosed with lung damage it's too late."

Later in February 2014 he wrote that he had tried to "smoke a little," had failed, and had learned he could not smoke at all, that quitting was not easy and he had gone through a program; in March 2014 he wrote that when he was addicted to cigarettes he ignored good medical advice.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own public account of tobacco dependence and of quitting through a program. Posted after the index date; recorded in the claims only.

claims.statement: At his death UPI reported that he had had COPD for over a year, that the disease resulted from years of smoking, and that he had called himself an "Olympic championship smoker" in a television interview.
claims.clinical_interpretation: News summary at his death; the length of his illness before the January 2014 disclosure is not otherwise documented.

claims.statement: He died at his home in Los Angeles on February 27, 2015, at 83; news reports citing his family gave the cause as end-stage chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Cause of death as reported publicly; recorded without further detail.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Confirm COPD with post-bronchodilator spirometry in an 82-year-old former smoker who quit about thirty years ago, classify it by GOLD 2013 (grade 3, group B) with the CAT, mMRC, and exacerbation history, start a long-acting bronchodilator pair in an inhaler he can use well, check blood eosinophils and alpha-1 antitrypsin, assess oxygen need at rest and on exertion, enroll him in pulmonary rehabilitation, bring vaccines up to date, explain why he is not eligible for lung cancer screening, screen for comorbidities and mood, and begin advance care planning, on the CMID COPD schedule.

documentation.chief_complaint: Four-week COPD review after starting tiotropium-olodaterol

hpi.narrative: Mr. Nimoy returns four weeks after starting tiotropium-olodaterol two inhalations each morning. He feels a little less tight in the chest in the mornings and has cut his albuterol from once or twice a day to about four times a week. He still has to stop for breath after about 100 meters on level ground. The dose counter shows no missed doses. He has had no flare-up, increase in sputum, fever, or need for antibiotics or prednisone. He has no dry mouth, difficulty passing urine, palpitations, or tremor. He saw the pulmonologist this morning, and his 6-minute walk test was done in the pulmonary function laboratory. He starts pulmonary rehabilitation next week.

documentation.chief_complaint: Three-month COPD review after pulmonary rehabilitation

hpi.narrative: Mr. Nimoy returns three months after starting tiotropium-olodaterol and four days after finishing pulmonary rehabilitation. He attended all 24 sessions. He now walks about 300 meters at his own pace before stopping, uses the pursed-lip breathing he learned there, and has a home program of walking twice a day and strength exercises three times a week. He uses albuterol about twice a week, mostly before longer walks. He has taken every maintenance dose. He has had no flare-up, antibiotic or prednisone course, or emergency visit. He repeated the 6-minute walk in the pulmonary function laboratory this morning. The pneumococcal vaccine that was out of stock at the last visit is available today.

The summer heat made him more breathless on a few afternoons, and he walked in the early morning instead.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Nimoy is an 83-year-old man with COPD (GOLD 3, group B) who returns for his subsequent annual wellness visit, eight weeks after his six-month COPD review. His last annual wellness visit was with his previous primary care clinician more than a year ago. He completed the health risk assessment before the visit. He takes tiotropium-olodaterol two inhalations each morning and uses albuterol about twice a week, mostly before longer walks. He has had no flare-ups, antibiotic or prednisone courses, emergency visits, or hospital stays since his first visit in February. He keeps up the home exercise program from pulmonary rehabilitation, walking about 15 minutes twice a day and doing leg and arm exercises three times a week. He has no new concerns.

documentation.advance_care_planning: Voluntary advance care planning discussion of about 25 minutes, with his consent. We talked about what COPD at this stage can mean over the coming years, including flare-ups that may need hospital care, and why it helps to plan ahead. He named a health care agent, and a health care proxy form was completed; the agent is recorded in the chart and is not named here. He said that what matters most to him is staying at home, keeping up his creative work, and being told plainly about his health so he can make his own decisions. He chose not to record specific treatment preferences today. The plan will be revisited yearly and after any hospital stay.

referral.question: COPD in an 82-year-old former smoker, now confirmed on spirometry as GOLD 3. Please confirm the grade and group, review the inhaler choice and the place of an inhaled corticosteroid, assess his oxygen needs, and advise on pulmonary rehabilitation and lung cancer screening
referral.pertinent_history: COPD diagnosed by his previous clinician without spirometry on file; he describes breathlessness that stops him after about 100 meters (mMRC 3) and uses a wheelchair at airports. CAT 22. No exacerbation, antibiotic or prednisone course, or hospital stay in the past 12 months. Smoked heavily for about 25 years (about 40 pack-years) and quit about 30 years ago; no occupational exposure. Spirometry today: post-bronchodilator FEV1 1.26 L (46 percent predicted), FVC 2.93 L, FEV1/FVC 0.43. Blood eosinophils 0.18 x10³/µL; alpha-1 antitrypsin 138 mg/dL; hemoglobin 14.6 g/dL. Resting saturation 93 percent. ECG in sinus rhythm. PHQ-9 3. Started tiotropium-olodaterol soft mist inhaler today, with albuterol as needed
questions: Do you agree with GOLD 3, group B, and is anything other than COPD contributing to his breathlessness?
Is a long-acting bronchodilator pair in a soft mist inhaler the right start, and is there any place for an inhaled corticosteroid?
Does he need oxygen at rest or on exertion?
Does the alpha-1 antitrypsin level need further testing, and does he need chest CT for emphysema, lung volume reduction, or lung cancer screening?
Should he start pulmonary rehabilitation now, and what should we watch for?

consultant_note.history: Mr. Nimoy is seen at the request of Dr. Benedetti four weeks after starting tiotropium-olodaterol. He smoked heavily for many years, quit about 30 years ago through a cessation program, and has been limited by breathlessness for some time. He now stops after about 100 meters on level ground. His mornings are a little easier on the new inhaler, and his albuterol use has fallen to about four times a week. He has little cough, a small amount of clear morning sputum, and no wheeze at rest, chest pain, orthopnea, ankle swelling, snoring, or reflux. He has had no exacerbation in the past year. He is keen to keep active and to warn others about smoking
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Intake spirometry before and after bronchodilator, the blood eosinophil count, the alpha-1 antitrypsin level, hemoglobin, creatinine, the intake ECG, the CAT and mMRC scores, and today's 6-minute walk test with continuous oximetry

exam.finding: Tall man, comfortable at rest, speaking in full sentences
Hyperinflated; reduced breath sounds throughout with prolonged expiration; no wheeze or crackles
Regular rhythm; no murmur; no raised jugular venous pressure or edema
No clubbing or cyanosis
Correct with the soft mist inhaler

assessment.assessment: Confirmed: post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 0.43 with FEV1 46 percent predicted is GOLD grade 3. CAT 19 today (22 at intake), mMRC 3, and no exacerbation in 12 months place him in group B. Normal hemoglobin, a normal ECG, and no signs of heart failure make another main cause of his breathlessness unlikely

Resting saturation 93 percent. On the 6-minute walk he covered 270 m with a lowest saturation of 89 percent. He meets no criterion for long-term oxygen, and the evidence does not support oxygen for moderate exertional desaturation; an arterial blood gas is not needed while resting saturation stays above 92 percent

138 mg/dL is normal, which excludes severe deficiency; no phenotyping is needed. He is not eligible for lung cancer screening, because he quit more than 15 years ago. Chest CT is not needed now: there is no suspected complication, and lung volume reduction would only be considered if he stayed severely limited after optimal treatment and rehabilitation

recommendations: Continue tiotropium-olodaterol two inhalations each morning, with albuterol as needed; the soft mist inhaler suits him because it needs no strong inspiratory effort

No inhaled corticosteroid: he has had no exacerbation and his eosinophils are below 300 per microliter. Reconsider after two moderate exacerbations or one hospital stay in a year if eosinophils are 100 or more
Pulmonary rehabilitation now, with a 6-minute walk at entry (done today) and at exit
No oxygen; check saturation at every visit and reassess if resting saturation falls to 92 percent or less
No further alpha-1 antitrypsin testing and no chest CT at present
PCV20 now, RSV vaccine before the next respiratory virus season, and yearly high-dose influenza and COVID-19 vaccines
Written action plan for flare-ups; spirometry yearly
consultant_note.communication: Discussed with Dr. Benedetti the same day; the patient agrees with the plan
consultant_note.follow_up: Primary care will continue monitoring on the CMID schedule. Pulmonology will see him again after any hospital stay for an exacerbation, two or more moderate exacerbations in a year, a fall in resting saturation to 92 percent or less, or loss of the benefit from rehabilitation
